subject: Agriculture
title: Rice: Feeding Half the World
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Rice: Feeding Half the World.

hook.text: Rice is the primary food for 3.5 billion people. In Asia, the word for rice often means 'food' itself.

buildup.text: Paddy rice grows in flooded fields. Standing water suppresses weeds and creates a unique aquatic ecosystem.

discovery.text: Flooded paddies also emit methane—rice cultivation accounts for roughly 10% of agricultural greenhouse gases.

twist.text: Alternate wetting and drying—draining paddies periodically—cuts methane by 50% without reducing yields.

climax.text: Scaling this simple technique across Asia could have a meaningful impact on global methane emissions.

punchline.text: Draining paddies halfway saves water and cuts methane. Simple works.

quiz.question: How much can alternate wetting and drying reduce rice methane emissions?

details.summary: Rice is the staple food for over 3.5 billion people, primarily in Asia and Africa. This topic covers paddy cultivation, the Green Revolution's impact on rice yields, and the challenges of sustaining production as water becomes scarcer and climates shift.
details.whyItMatters: Rice provides more dietary calories to humans than any other crop. Disruptions to rice production—from floods, drought, or policy—directly threaten food security for billions.
takeaways: Rice paddies account for about 12% of global agricultural land use
Asia produces and consumes over 90% of the world's rice supply
Flooded rice paddies emit significant methane, a potent greenhouse gas

faq.question: Why is rice so important globally as a food crop?
faq.answer: Rice provides around 20% of all dietary calories consumed by humans. It is the primary staple for over 3.5 billion people across Asia, Africa, and Latin America, making it the single most important food crop for human nutrition.

faq.question: What environmental challenges does rice farming face?
faq.answer: Rice paddies require large amounts of water and emit methane from flooded soils. Climate change threatens yields through higher temperatures, erratic rainfall, sea-level rise in coastal deltas, and increasing frequency of droughts.
